title: Private deployment networking incident notes (VPC peering / DNS / TLS / egress)
content:
Context:
- Private deployment (customer: AcmeCorp) spun up in us-west-2 VPC. We started seeing 504/connection timeouts from the control-plane agent to the model runtime nodes around 2025-02-13 18:22 PST. Customer reported degraded inference and failed healthchecks in the console.

Goal: capture commands tried, error snippets, hypotheses and next steps for handoff to SRE/Networking. This is a personal scratchpad / breadcrumbs doc.

Timeline / quick summary:
- 18:10 - Initial alert: control-plane -> runtime healthchecks failing (503/timeout)
- 18:14 - Confirmed some pods on runtime cluster show CrashLoopBackOff (but many are Running)
- 18:20 - Observed TCP connection resets when control-plane attempts mutual TLS handshake with runtime agent
- 18:30 - Found intermittent DNS resolution failures for runtime node hostnames from the control plane
- 19:00 - SRE engaged; started testing VPC peering and route tables

Commands & raw outputs (copied from terminals):

1) Basic connectivity checks from control-plane bastion to runtime node IPs:
$ ping -c 3 10.2.45.12
PING 10.2.45.12 (10.2.45.12) 56(84) bytes of data.
--- 10.2.45.12 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 2002ms

2) Traceroute to see where packets drop (from control-plane subnet 10.1.0.0/16 to runtime 10.2.0.0/16):
$ traceroute -n 10.2.45.12
traceroute to 10.2.45.12 (10.2.45.12), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  10.1.0.1  0.700 ms  0.556 ms  0.534 ms
 2  10.254.1.1  1.101 ms  1.087 ms  1.056 ms
 3  * * *
(drops after transit gateway / peering hop)

3) nslookup / dig from control plane for runtime service DNS name (runtime.service.acmecorp.internal):
$ dig +short runtime-45.acmecorp.internal @10.1.2.5
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

4) curl mTLS errors observed when control-plane hits runtime-agent endpoint (kube service IP / nodeport):
$ curl -v --cert client.crt --key client.key https://10.2.45.12:8443/healthz
* Connected to 10.2.45.12 (10.2.45.12) port 8443 (#0)
* TLS 1.2 connection using TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
* Server certificate: CN=runtime-agent.acmecorp.internal
* Closing connection 0
curl: (56) OpenSSL SSL_read: Connection was reset, errno 104

5) tcpdump on control-plane bastion during attempt (short capture):
$ sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 host 10.2.45.12 and port 8443 -w capture.pcap
(Observed TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, then RST from remote)

6) VPC peering and route checks (from control-plane account):
$ aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=status-code,Values=active
{
      "VpcPeeringConnections": [ { /* truncated */ } ]
    }
(peering connection ACTIVE)

$ aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0a1b2c3d
(route to 10.2.0.0/16 via pcx-07abcd) - looks present in control-plane route table

7) On runtime side (node) - resolution sometimes works locally: 
$ getent hosts runtime-45.acmecorp.internal
10.2.45.12 runtime-45.acmecorp.internal
(so node's own resolver / /etc/hosts works; control-plane resolver hitting customer DNS fails intermittently)

Hypotheses so far:
- Hypothesis A: Asymmetric route / missing return path from runtime VPC to control-plane subnet causing TCP RSTs. Evidence: traceroute drops after the peering hop; ping 100% loss. But peering status shows ACTIVE and route table entries exist. Need to check security groups and NACLs.

- Hypothesis B: DNS recursion/forwarder unhealthy in customer VPC (10.1.2.5) causing intermittent resolution failures; control-plane falls back to IP which sometimes fails due to ephemeral network issues. Evidence: dig to the forwarder times out, but local getent on node works. Could be Route53 Resolver endpoints or firewall blocking UDP/TCP 53 from control-plane.

- Hypothesis C: TLS handshake issues due to MTU / packet fragmentation across transit gateway causing handshake to reset mid-way. Evidence: OpenSSL reports SSL_read reset; tcpdump shows RST after handshake. Need to check MSS/MTU and if there's `DF` set.

Quick checks to run next (ordered):
1) From control-plane, run mtr -n --report 10.2.45.12 to get loss per-hop over time (30s)
2) Check Security Groups on runtime nodes: ensure port 8443 allowed from control-plane security group (not just CIDR). Confirm SG references (peer SG) are correct.
3) Check NACLs on both VPCs for ephemeral ports / return trafffic; confirm rule order and deny catch-alls.
4) Validate Route53 Resolver outbound endpoint and rule associations: ensure control-plane can resolve internal hostnames; check status in customer account.
5) Try curl with --ciphers and --tlsv1.2 and increasing verbosity and capture with `openssl s_client -connect 10.2.45.12:8443 -cert client.crt -key client.key -showcerts` to see handshake details.
6) Reproduce from another az / node in control-plane VPC to rule out single-bastion issues.
7) Temporary mitigation: set control-plane to fall back to runtime HTTP gateway via region-internal public LB (if customer allows) to restore traffic while debugging peering.

Notes from SRE call (19:25):
- SRE suspects NACL issue: NACL in runtime VPC had an explicit deny for high ephemeral ports due to previous 'cleanup' script. Diego to audit NACL history and revert if confirmed.
    "- Priya to check Route53 Resolver endpoints and CloudWatch logs for DNS timeouts around 18:20-18:40.

Open items for handoff:
- Diego: confirm NACL rules, post before/after and if revert restores connectivity.
- Priya: export Route53 resolver logs and paste relevant time slices (18:10-19:00).
- Me (Maya): run mtr and openssl s_client captures, upload pcap to the incident ticket, and try curl from a different control-plane AZ.

Decision log / relevant acronyms:
- We will NOT immediately tear down the peering connection. Instead we will audit ACLs and security groups first.
- If NACL revert fixes it, root cause likely an accidental deny rule. If not, escalate to AWS TAC for transit gateway / MTU weirdness.

Appendix: useful commands saved here for quick copy-paste:
- mtr: mtr -n --report 10.2.45.12
- tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 host 10.2.45.12 and port 8443 -w /tmp/rt-8443.pcap
- openssl client: openssl s_client -connect 10.2.45.12:8443 -cert client.crt -key client.key -state -debug
- check NACLs: aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filter Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0b2c3d4e
- check SGs: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0abc1234
- route tables: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0a1b2c3d

End notes / TODO: convert interesting bits to incident timeline in Jira and attach pcap + mtr output. Keep this doc as a living scratchpad.
